items.requirement: A tenant-visible audit log records team and platform-admin actions (settings, prompt and knowledge-base edits, exports, deletions, role changes, impersonation); it is kept at least 12 months and can be exported. Each conversation has an agent tool-call trace (model, prompt version, tool, arguments, result) for disputes.
items.why: Businesses need to see who changed what and why the agent acted, both for trust and for GDPR accountability.
items.source: OWASP ASVS 5.0 V16.3.3; OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 ASI10; SOC 2 CC7.2
items.how_to_verify: Perform an action and see it in the tenant audit UI. Open a conversation and inspect its trace. Test the export.

items.requirement: No secrets appear in source, git history, container images, CI logs or client bundles (NEXT_PUBLIC_* included). Secret scanning runs as GitHub push protection plus gitleaks or trufflehog in CI, a full-history scan is done before launch, and any secret found is rotated.
items.why: Leaked PSP, telephony or LLM keys give immediate financial and data access.
items.source: OWASP ASVS 5.0 V13.3.1; OWASP Top 10:2025 A02 Security Misconfiguration; anthropics/claude-code-security-review category 'Hardcoded API keys, passwords, or tokens'
items.how_to_verify: gitleaks over the full history reports 0 findings. Push protection is enabled in repository settings. Scan the .next/static and image layers for key patterns.

items.requirement: All backend secrets live in Render secret environment groups or a vault, separate per environment, with access limited to production deployers and never shared by chat or email. Provider keys are scoped (Stripe restricted keys, scoped ElevenLabs and Twilio API keys).
items.why: Broad, shared or cross-environment secrets turn one leak into full compromise.
items.how_to_verify: Review the access list of the Render environment groups. The Stripe dashboard shows restricted keys only. Confirm that staging keys fail against production.

items.requirement: Configuration fails closed. The app refuses to start when required secrets or settings are missing, empty, placeholder-like or too short; there are no os.getenv('SECRET', 'dev')-style fallbacks. Security toggles default to secure (auth required, debug off, CORS deny, Secure cookies). Zero or negative values for limits and TTLs are rejected rather than meaning 'unlimited'.
items.why: Fallback secrets and fail-open defaults are among the most common real-world misconfigurations that reach production.
items.source: Trail of Bits insecure-defaults (fallback-secrets, fail-open-security, debug-features); Trail of Bits sharp-edges (dangerous defaults, configuration cliffs); OWASP ASVS 5.0 V13.4.2; OWASP Top 10:2025 A02
items.how_to_verify: Start the app with each required variable unset or empty and expect a non-zero exit. A Semgrep rule flags getenv with a default on secret-like names. Config unit tests with values 0 and -1.

items.requirement: Tenant integration credentials (Google OAuth refresh tokens, Meta and WhatsApp tokens, Telegram bot tokens, telephony credentials, PSP keys and webhook secrets) use application-level envelope encryption (KMS-managed key, AES-GCM). They are write-only through the API, decrypted only in the worker that uses them, and revoked and deleted when disconnected or at tenant offboarding.
items.why: A DB dump or SQL injection must not hand over every tenant's third-party accounts.
items.how_to_verify: The DB column holds ciphertext. GET on the integration returns a masked value. Disconnecting revokes the token at the provider (provider API check).

items.requirement: A documented rotation schedule (for example at most 12 months for long-lived keys, and immediately on suspected exposure or the departure of anyone with access) uses a tested zero-downtime procedure, including dual-key acceptance for session and webhook signing keys.
items.why: Keys that are never rotated keep breaches and ex-staff access alive indefinitely.
items.how_to_verify: The rotation log has dates per key. A rotation drill in staging completes with zero failed requests.

items.requirement: Production hardening: debug modes and tracebacks are off; FastAPI docs are disabled or protected; neither .git nor public source maps are exposed (source maps go privately to the error tracker); TLS 1.2+ only with valid certificates; the DB and Redis require TLS and authentication with least-privilege roles; there are no default credentials; internal services are not publicly reachable.
items.why: Debug output, exposed metadata and open internal services hand attackers reconnaissance or direct access.
items.source: OWASP ASVS 5.0 V13.4.1, V13.4.2, V13.4.5, V12.1.1, V12.3.1, V13.2.2, V13.2.3, V16.5.1; Trail of Bits insecure-defaults (debug-features, default-credentials)
items.how_to_verify: curl production for /.git/HEAD, *.map and /docs and expect 404. testssl.sh grade A. A DB connection without sslmode=require is refused. A forced 500 returns a generic error without a stack trace.

items.requirement: Lockfiles (uv.lock, package-lock or pnpm-lock) are committed and CI installs from them frozen. Automated vulnerability scanning (pip-audit or osv-scanner, npm audit, Dependabot or Renovate) blocks critical and high findings within documented remediation SLAs (for example critical within 7 days, high within 30). A CycloneDX SBOM is produced for each release.
items.why: Vulnerable or drifting dependencies are now a top-three application risk.
items.source: OWASP ASVS 5.0 V15.1.1, V15.1.2, V15.2.1; OWASP Top 10:2025 A03 Software Supply Chain Failures
items.how_to_verify: CI logs show a frozen install and the scan step. An SBOM artifact is attached to each release. An open-vulnerability age report sits within the SLAs.

items.requirement: Every new direct dependency is reviewed using registry-measured data, not guesses: maintenance status or archival, publisher concentration, install-time scripts, typosquatting, licence. npm ci --ignore-scripts is used where the build allows.
items.why: Abandoned, hijacked or typosquatted packages are a common route to malicious code in builds.
items.source: Trail of Bits supply-chain-risk-auditor; OWASP Top 10:2025 A03
items.how_to_verify: The PR template has a dependency checkbox, and the supply-chain collector report is attached for PRs that add dependencies.

items.requirement: CI/CD integrity: GitHub Actions are pinned to full commit SHAs; workflow permissions are least-privilege (contents: read by default); there is no pull_request_target workflow that checks out the PR head; secrets are unavailable to fork PRs; deploy credentials use OIDC rather than long-lived tokens; production deploys go through a protected environment.
items.why: A compromised workflow or action can steal production secrets or ship malicious builds.
items.source: OWASP Top 10:2025 A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures, A03; Trail of Bits agentic-actions-auditor Vector D (pull_request_target + checkout); SLSA v1.0 Build L2
items.how_to_verify: zizmor and actionlint scans over .github/workflows come back clean. Review the repository and environment protection settings.

items.requirement: Where AI agents run in CI/CD (Claude Code Action, Codex, Gemini CLI): attacker-controlled event data (issue and PR titles and bodies, comments, commit messages, CI error logs, workflow_dispatch inputs) never reaches prompts directly or through env-var intermediaries without trust gating; Bash(*), --yolo, danger-full-access and wildcard allowed-user lists are not used; AI output is never eval'd in run steps; agents get read-only tokens unless write is needed.
items.why: Prompt injection through repository events can make a CI agent exfiltrate secrets or push malicious code.
items.source: Trail of Bits agentic-actions-auditor Vectors A–I; OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 LLM01; OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 ASI02
items.how_to_verify: Run the agentic-actions-auditor methodology over all workflows and expect no Medium or High findings. Review the env blocks feeding prompt fields.

items.requirement: Branch protection and change management: main is protected (PR required; CODEOWNERS review by someone other than the author for security-sensitive paths; required checks for tests, lint, type-check, SAST and dependency scan). Direct and force pushes are blocked. Production deploys only from main through CI, with a traceable commit-to-release mapping.
items.why: Unreviewed changes to auth, payments or tenant scoping are how regressions and insider risk reach production.
items.how_to_verify: Export the branch protection settings. A direct push to main is rejected. The release notes link the deployed SHA.

items.requirement: Security testing: SAST on every PR (Semgrep with --metrics=off including third-party rulesets, and/or CodeQL) with triaged findings, where zero findings is investigated rather than assumed clean. High-risk changes (auth, crypto, payments, webhooks, tenant scoping, agent tools) get a security-focused differential review covering injection, authorization bypass, crypto and secrets, deserialization and data exposure, with blast radius and test coverage. An external penetration test is done before first sale and then yearly.
items.why: Automated and focused reviews catch exploitable bugs that functional tests never exercise.
items.source: Trail of Bits static-analysis (semgrep, codeql, sarif-parsing); Trail of Bits differential-review; anthropics/claude-code-security-review security categories; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.8.29
items.how_to_verify: SARIF uploads are visible in GitHub code scanning. Review reports are attached to high-risk PRs. The pentest report and remediation tracker are on file.

items.requirement: Property-based tests cover invariant-heavy code: phone and email normalizers (idempotence), DTO serialization roundtrips, deposit and money arithmetic (Decimal, never negative), slot allocation (no overlaps or double booking), timezone and DST conversion, webhook signature verification (rejects any mutated payload) and rate-limiter arithmetic.
items.why: Example tests miss the edge cases (DST, Unicode, boundaries) where booking and payment bugs hide.
items.source: Trail of Bits property-based-testing (roundtrip, idempotence, invariant properties); OWASP ASVS 5.0 V2.3.4
items.how_to_verify: Hypothesis tests exist and run in CI. Deliberately breaking a normalizer makes a property test fail.

items.requirement: RPO and RTO are defined and published to customers in the SLA, for example RPO of at most 15 min through Postgres PITR/WAL, RTO of at most 4 h for the full platform, and at most 15 min to switch on call forwarding as a fallback.
items.why: Without targets, backup and failover design cannot be verified and customers cannot plan.
items.how_to_verify: The SLA and BCP documents state the targets, and the backup and PITR configuration matches them.

items.requirement: Managed Postgres PITR plus daily logical backups are copied off-platform to a separate account with separate credentials in an EU region, encrypted and immutable (object lock or versioning) for the retention window. Object-storage recordings are either included or explicitly excluded in the documentation. Backup failures alert.
items.why: Ransomware, account compromise or a provider incident can destroy both production and same-account backups.
items.how_to_verify: Review the backup inventory. Attempting to delete a backup with app or deploy credentials is denied. Test the backup-failure alert.

items.requirement: At least once a quarter, a full restore goes into an isolated environment. The achieved RPO and RTO are measured, data integrity is checked (row counts, sample tenant queries, recordings reachable), the evidence is documented, and the runbook is updated.
items.why: Untested backups regularly turn out to be unrestorable at the moment they are needed.
items.how_to_verify: The latest restore-test report is no more than 90 days old and records timings and integrity checks.

items.requirement: Timeouts and circuit breakers protect calls to the LLM, voice, telephony, messaging, PSP and calendar services. A secondary LLM provider or model is configured and tested. When the agent is down, the widget shows the business's contact details and takes a message for callback. Queued notifications retry with backoff, jitter and idempotency.
items.why: Single-provider dependencies on LLM and voice vendors make their outages your outage.
items.source: OWASP ASVS 5.0 V16.5.2, V16.5.3; OWASP Top 10:2025 A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions; OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 ASI08
items.how_to_verify: Fault-injection tests per dependency in staging (timeouts, 5xx, DNS failure) end in the documented degraded behavior. Keep failover drill evidence.

items.requirement: SLIs and SLOs are defined for call answer success, agent response latency (p95), chat availability, booking success, notification delivery and API availability, with targets (for example 99.9% monthly), dashboards, and an error-budget policy that drives release freezes.
items.why: SLOs turn 'the AI felt slow' into measurable commitments and prioritization.
items.source: Google SRE Book ch. 4 'Service Level Objectives'; SOC 2 A1.1
items.how_to_verify: The SLO dashboard exists, and the monthly SLO report is shared internally.

items.requirement: A public status page shows each component (voice, chat, messengers, cabinet, payments) and offers email subscription. Incident communication templates exist in IT and EN. Maintenance is announced at least 72 h ahead. Major incidents get a published post-incident report.
items.why: Businesses lose bookings during outages and need timely, honest communication to keep trust.
items.how_to_verify: The status page URL is live. The templates exist. The last major-incident report is published.

items.requirement: An incident response plan defines roles (incident commander, communications, scribe), a severity matrix, 24/7 contact paths, playbooks (credential leak, cross-tenant exposure, toll fraud, prompt-injection abuse, PSP or webhook compromise), evidence collection, notification clocks (GDPR 72 h, tenant contractual deadlines, PSP), and post-mortems with tracked actions. A tabletop exercise runs every year.
items.why: Improvised incident handling causes missed legal deadlines and prolonged damage.
items.how_to_verify: The IR plan document exists, a tabletop record is no more than 12 months old, and post-mortem actions are tracked to closure.

items.requirement: Release safety and capacity: DB migrations are backward-compatible (expand/contract) and tested on a production-sized copy; rollouts are staged behind feature flags; rollback takes one step; per-tenant concurrency and rate quotas prevent noisy neighbours; a load test runs before onboarding large tenants; dev, staging and prod are separated (accounts, data, keys).
items.why: Bad migrations and capacity surprises are the most common self-inflicted outages.
items.how_to_verify: Rollback drill evidence, a load-test report, and quota configuration. Staging keys cannot reach production resources.

items.requirement: The customer contract set consists of Terms of Service, DPA, SLA (availability, support, RPO/RTO, credits), an Acceptable Use Policy (no spam, unlawful telemarketing, impersonation or voice cloning without consent), tenant obligations (privacy notices, lawful basis and consent, AI-disclosure duties as deployer) and liability caps, in Italian and English. Onerous clauses get separate specific approval at signup.
items.why: The platform's legal position on consent, AI disclosure and abuse depends on clearly allocating duties to tenants, and Italian law requires specific approval of onerous standard clauses.
items.source: GDPR Art. 28; Codice privacy art. 130; EU AI Act Art. 50; Codice civile art. 1341-1342
items.how_to_verify: Legal review sign-off. The signup flow records acceptance plus the separate checkbox for c.c. art. 1341(2) clauses, with the version.

items.requirement: A vendor register records data categories, location, DPA, security attestations (SOC 2 or ISO 27001 reports), criticality and exit plan for every vendor. A vendor is assessed before onboarding and reviewed every year.
items.why: A security failure at the LLM, voice, telephony or hosting vendor is a direct breach of the platform's own obligations.
items.source: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.5.19–A.5.22; SOC 2 CC9.2; GDPR Art. 28(1); NIS2 Directive (EU) 2022/2555 Art. 21(2)(d) (customer supply-chain expectations)
items.how_to_verify: The register has review dates within 12 months. Attestation reports are on file for critical vendors.

items.requirement: Every quarter, review who can access production, Render, the DB, object storage, GitHub admin, the PSP, telephony, LLM and voice consoles, DNS and the registrar, email-domain admin and the password manager. MFA is enforced on every console, unused accounts are removed, and evidence is kept.
items.why: Access creep and unused accounts are a leading cause of breaches in small teams.
items.how_to_verify: The latest access-review record is no more than 90 days old. MFA coverage report is 100% across consoles.

items.requirement: Joiners get least-privilege access and security plus AI-literacy training. Leavers are offboarded within 24 h of departure: SSO and accounts disabled, tokens, SSH and API keys revoked, shared secrets they knew rotated, repo and document ownership transferred, devices recovered, all evidenced.
items.why: Ex-staff access to telephony, PSP or production consoles is a severe and common exposure.
items.how_to_verify: The offboarding ticket has timestamps for each step. Vendor consoles show the user removed. The secret rotation log matches.

items.requirement: ISMS basics: an information security policy, a risk register covering AI, telephony fraud, payments and privacy risks that is reviewed at least yearly, an asset inventory, and staff policy acknowledgments. A roadmap to SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 as customers require, and a security questionnaire and trust page ready for buyers.
items.why: B2B buyers, especially hotels and chains, require evidence of a managed security program before purchase.
items.source: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clauses 5–6, A.5.1, A.5.9; SOC 2 CC3.1–CC3.4
items.how_to_verify: The risk register review date is no more than 12 months old. The policy set and acknowledgments are on file. The trust page is published.

items.requirement: Staff (support, sales, engineering) are trained on the AI system's capabilities and limits, prompt-injection and social-engineering risks, and data protection, with records kept. Tenant onboarding includes AI-use guidance for their own staff as deployers.
items.why: The AI Act still requires providers and deployers to support AI literacy (reworded by the Digital Omnibus), and trained staff are the main defense against social engineering.
items.source: EU AI Act Art. 4 (as amended by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744); ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.6.3
items.how_to_verify: Training records per employee. Onboarding materials for tenants are published.

items.requirement: Contracts allow exit with at most 2 months' notice and a transitional period of at most 30 days with service continuing. During it, all exportable data (bookings, customers, conversations, recordings, transcripts, knowledge base, configuration) can be exported in structured, commonly used, machine-readable formats via a documented API or UI. A retrieval period of at least 30 days follows, then complete erasure with confirmation. Switching procedures and formats are disclosed before contracting. No switching charges apply from 12 Jan 2027, and only cost-based charges before that.
items.why: Data Act Chapter VI switching duties have applied to SaaS since 12 Sep 2025, and the Omnibus SME relief is still a proposal.
items.source: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 (Data Act) Art. 23, 25, 26, 29; GDPR Art. 28(3)(g)
items.how_to_verify: Contract clause review. An end-to-end export of a test tenant can be re-imported or validated as complete, and the deletion certificate is generated.

items.requirement: A regulatory applicability register documents assessments for: NIS2 (size-cap test, Italian D.Lgs. 138/2024, ACN registration if thresholds are crossed or the entity is designated); the Cyber Resilience Act (only if apps or plugins are distributed; reporting from 11 Sep 2026); EAA micro-enterprise status; AI Act role; DPO need; and PCI role. It is reviewed yearly and whenever headcount or turnover changes. A vulnerability disclosure policy and /.well-known/security.txt are published.
items.why: A micro SaaS is usually outside NIS2 and the CRA today, but crossing a threshold or shipping a client app changes obligations without warning.
items.source: NIS2 Directive (EU) 2022/2555 Art. 2, 21, 23; D.Lgs. 4 Sep 2024 n. 138; Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (CRA) Art. 14, 71; EAA Art. 4(5); GDPR Art. 37; RFC 9116
items.how_to_verify: The register document has a review date. security.txt is reachable and contains a valid Expires field.

items.requirement: Credential stuffing and brute-force defense: throttling per account and per IP or ASN with progressive delays, breached-password checks, a bot challenge (for example Turnstile) on anomalies, and MFA. Login, reset and signup give generic messages with equal timing so accounts cannot be enumerated. Spikes raise alerts.
items.why: Automated login attacks against SaaS cabinets are constant, and enumeration helps target owners.
items.source: OWASP ASVS 5.0 V6.1.1, V6.3.1, V6.3.8 (L3, adopted); OWASP Automated Threats OAT-007 Credential Cracking, OAT-008 Credential Stuffing; OWASP Top 10:2025 A07
items.how_to_verify: Script 1,000 attempts across accounts from rotating IPs and confirm they are throttled or challenged and an alert fires. Responses for existing and non-existing emails are identical in body, status and timing (within noise).

items.requirement: Rate limiting is correct. The client IP comes only from trusted proxy hops (Render or CDN X-Forwarded-For handling) and cannot be spoofed with client headers. Anonymous limits cannot be bypassed by adding an arbitrary Authorization header or rotating session IDs. Limits are keyed by IP, tenant, route and identity and stored centrally (for example Redis) across instances.
items.why: Rate limits that trust spoofable headers or reset per instance give a false sense of protection for every other abuse control.
items.source: OWASP ASVS 5.0 V15.3.4, V2.4.1; OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 API4; Trail of Bits sharp-edges (configuration cliffs)
items.how_to_verify: Requests with forged X-Forwarded-For values or a bogus Authorization header are still limited. A multi-instance test confirms the shared counter.

items.requirement: Public widget, hosted chat and messenger anti-automation: message rate limits per session, IP and tenant; message length caps; a maximum of new conversations per IP per hour; a bot challenge on anomalous patterns; a cost cap per session; blocking of abusive IPs. The agent cannot be used as a free general-purpose LLM (topic restriction).
items.why: An anonymous AI chat endpoint is a magnet for scraping, spam and free-LLM abuse at the tenant's and platform's expense.
items.source: OWASP ASVS 5.0 V2.4.1; OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 API4, API6; OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 LLM10
items.how_to_verify: A load script opening 1,000 conversations is throttled. Off-topic jailbreak evals ('write my thesis') are refused.

items.requirement: Fake bookings and denial of inventory: unconfirmed holds are limited per phone, email and IP and expire automatically; verification (SMS or email link) or a deposit is required above party-size or peak thresholds; tenants can keep a blocklist with GDPR-compliant retention; mass bookings or cancellations trigger anomaly alerts.
items.why: Bots or competitors can hold all slots and cause real revenue loss for restaurants and salons.
items.source: OWASP Automated Threats OAT-021 Denial of Inventory; OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 API6; OWASP ASVS 5.0 V2.3.2
items.how_to_verify: A script making 50 bookings from one number is blocked after the threshold. Pending holds expire on schedule. Test the alert.

items.requirement: Signup and tenant abuse controls: email verification and bot protection at signup. Phone-number provisioning and outbound calls or SMS are enabled only after business verification and a payment method on file. Trials are capped on minutes, messages and destinations. Tenants with high complaint, bounce or opt-out rates are reviewed and suspended automatically.
items.why: Fraudsters sign up to SaaS platforms to run toll fraud, phishing or spam campaigns under the platform's numbers and reputation.
items.source: OWASP Automated Threats OAT-019 Account Creation; CFCA fraud survey (IRSF via trial abuse); Gmail/Yahoo bulk-sender requirements (spam-rate threshold)
items.how_to_verify: A new unverified tenant cannot place an outbound international call or send SMS. In staging, crossing the complaint-rate threshold triggers suspension.

items.requirement: Outbound email reputation: SPF, DKIM (2048-bit) and DMARC (p=quarantine or reject) are aligned on sending domains. Per-tenant sending subdomains or a From-name policy stop tenants spoofing other brands. Links in tenant-authored campaigns are scanned for phishing, and bounces and complaints are processed.
items.why: Poor authentication or abusive tenants get the platform's sending domains blocklisted, which breaks booking confirmations for everyone.
items.source: Gmail/Yahoo bulk-sender requirements (2024); RFC 7489 (DMARC); Codice privacy art. 130(5)
items.how_to_verify: DNS checks of the SPF, DKIM and DMARC records. A mail-tester score of at least 9/10. A seeded known-phishing URL in a campaign is blocked.
